## 3D renders with `brainconn()`

`brainconn()` draws a connectivity matrix as a static 3D render in the style of BrainNet Viewer: nodes are spheres, edges are tubes, and the brain is a translucent glass surface. It returns a ggplot object, so you can save it with `ggsave()` or combine it with other plots.

The minimum input is an atlas and a connectivity matrix whose rows and columns match the regions of the atlas. Nodes are coloured by network, using the standard Yeo colours for Yeo/Schaefer networks (see `network_colors()`).

```{r, fig.width=6, fig.height=6, out.width='60%', message=FALSE}
library(brainconn)
x <- example_unweighted_undirected
brainconn(atlas = "schaefer300_n7", conmat = x, view = "top")
```

The `view` can be `"top"`, `"bottom"`, `"left"`, `"right"`, `"front"`, `"back"`, `"ortho"` (top, left and front together), `"all"` (all six), or any angle as `c(azimuth, elevation)` in degrees. In the top, bottom, front and back views the subject's left hemisphere is always on the left, marked with "L" and "R".

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=7, out.width='90%', message=FALSE}
brainconn(atlas = "schaefer300_n7", conmat = x, view = "ortho")
```

For weighted matrices, edge width shows the weight by default. Set `edge.color.weighted = TRUE` to colour edges by weight instead; signed weights use a blue-white-red palette centred on zero. Directed matrices are drawn with arrowheads.

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=6, out.width='70%', message=FALSE}
brainconn(atlas = "schaefer300_n7", conmat = example_weighted_undirected,
          view = "left", edge.color.weighted = TRUE, edge.width = 1.5)
brainconn(atlas = "schaefer300_n7", conmat = example_weighted_directed,
          view = c(-60, 20), labels = TRUE)
```

The look of the brain surface is controlled with `mesh.color` and `mesh.alpha`, and `mesh = NULL` removes it. Image size and anti-aliasing are set with `res` and `quality`.

## 2D plots with `brainconn2d()`
The `brainconn2d()` function (called `brainconn()` before version 1.0.0) allows users to input a binary/weighted and directed/directed (i.e. symmetric) connectivity matrix which can be plotted in MNI space onto several brain atlases provided with the package, or a user defined custom atlas. The layout of the nodes and edges is created using [ggraph](https://github.com/thomasp85/ggraph), which does most of the heavy lifting here. The background is a `custom_annotation` using [ggplot2](https://github.com/tidyverse/ggplot2). 

The minimum user input requirements for the `brainconn2d()` function is a connectivity matrix. This can be read into `r` as a matrix or data.fame. Some example connectivity matrices can be found in the `data/example` folder. The number of rows & columns should match the number of regions in the selected atlas. Custom atlases can also be used, see [Using custom atlases]. 

By default, the `view` is a top view, the `node.color` is by network.

In the `top`, `bottom`, `front` and `back` views the subject's left hemisphere is always on the left of the plot. "L" and "R" labels mark the hemispheres in these views; turn them off with `hemi.labels = FALSE`.

```{r, out.width='50%', warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(brainconn)
x <- example_unweighted_undirected
brainconn2d(atlas ="schaefer300_n7", conmat=x, node.size = 3, view="ortho")
```



You can change the default view, node, edge and background properties as well as show all nodes of the atlas, rather than just the ones that have connected edges.  
```{r, out.width='50%', warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
brainconn2d(atlas ="schaefer300_n7", conmat=example_unweighted_undirected, view="left", node.size = 3, node.color = "hotpink", edge.width = 2, edge.color="darkblue", edge.alpha = 0.8, all.nodes = T, show.legend = F)
```

If the connectivity matrix you input is not a binary matrix, i.e. the values are weighted, by default `brainconn2d()` will modulate the `edge.width` by the weighted values. `scale.edge.width` can be used to scale the edge width.

```{r, out.width='50%',  warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
x <- example_weighted_undirected

brainconn2d(atlas ="schaefer300_n7", conmat=x, node.size = 5,view="bottom", scale.edge.width = c(1,3), background.alpha = 0.4, show.legend = F)
```

You can also color the edges by weight using the `edge.color.weighted` option.

```{r, out.width='50%',  warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

brainconn2d(atlas ="schaefer300_n7", conmat=example_weighted_undirected, node.size = 7,view="bottom", edge.width = 2, edge.color.weighted = T, show.legend = T)
```

If the input is a directed matrix (i.e. non-symmetrical), the edges will be displayed as directed arrows, with the `edge.width` and `edge.color` serving the same purpose:

```{r, out.width='50%',  warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
x <- example_unweighted_directed

brainconn2d(atlas ="schaefer300_n7", conmat=x, node.size = 4, view="right", edge.alpha = 0.6)
```

Weighted and directed matrix example:
```{r, out.width='50%',  warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
x <- example_weighted_directed

brainconn2d(atlas ="schaefer300_n7", conmat=x, view="front", edge.color.weighted=T)
```


You can auto add `labels`, but this doesn't work to great if theirs a large number of edges. 
```{r, out.width='50%',  warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
brainconn2d(atlas ="schaefer300_n7", conmat=example_unweighted_undirected, labels = T, label.size = 2, node.size = 3)
```

If you want to weight the nodes by a feature such as degree, you can provide a vector the length of the number of ROIs in the parcellation to `node.size`: 

```{r, out.width='50%',  warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
x <- example_unweighted_undirected
x_igraph <- igraph::graph_from_adjacency_matrix(as.matrix(example_unweighted_undirected)) #convert connectivity matrix into an graph object.
d <- igraph::degree(x_igraph) #use igraph::degree to obtain a vector of nodal degree
d <- d[d != 0] #remove nodes with no edges 
brainconn2d(atlas ="schaefer300_n7", conmat=x, node.size = d)
```



## Basic use of `brainconn3D()`
`brainconn3D()` draws an interactive 3D plot that you can rotate and zoom. It accepts the same kinds of connectivity matrices as `brainconn()`. Every non-zero edge is drawn as a line; edge directions are not shown. 

```{r, out.width='50%',  warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
p <- brainconn3D(atlas ="schaefer300_n7", conmat=example_unweighted_undirected, show.legend = F)
p
```

Modifiable features include `node.color`, `node.size`, `edge.size` & `edge.width`, brain surface `opacity` and `d.factor` (a multiplication factor to control the spread of nodes.)
```{r, out.width='50%',  warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
p <- brainconn3D(atlas = "schaefer300_n7", conmat=example_unweighted_undirected, edge.width = 6, edge.color = "green", node.size = 8, node.color = "red", show.legend = F)
p
```


### Highlighting connections

With `highlight = TRUE`, hovering over a node highlights its edges and neighbouring nodes and greys out the rest. Clicking a node keeps it highlighted until you click it again or click the brain. Hovering over any node shows its network, degree, strength and strongest connections. Edges can also be coloured by weight with `edge.color.weighted = TRUE`.

```{r, out.width='70%', warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
brainconn3D(atlas = "schaefer300_n7", conmat = example_weighted_undirected,
            edge.color.weighted = TRUE, highlight = TRUE, show.legend = TRUE)
```

The `d.factor` can be adjusted for different purposes. The default is set to 1.05.
```{r, out.width='50%',  warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
p <- brainconn3D(atlas ="schaefer300_n7", conmat=example_unweighted_undirected, edge.width = 3, edge.color = "brown", node.size = 3, d.factor = 1.3, all.nodes = T, opacity = 0.3, show.legend = F)
p
```

## Using custom atlases

To use you own atlas, you will require a data.frame with a minimum of four column: "ROI.name", "x.mni", "y.mni", "z.mni". You can also include a "network" column for node-coloring purposes. The x y and z.mni columns are the centroid coordinates for each roi in MNI space. These coordinates will sometimes be published with the atlas, and can also be obtained from the atlas .nii file. One way of doing this would be with FSL e.g.`fslstats roi.nii -c`.

To check that your custom atlas matches the requirements for `brainconn()`, `brainconn2d()` or `brainconn3D()`, you can use the `check_atlas()` function:

```{r, out.width='50%',  warning=FALSE, message=TRUE}
custom_atlas <- custom_atlas_example
check_atlas(custom_atlas)

brainconn(atlas = custom_atlas, conmat = example_unweighted_undirected,
          node.color = "black", view = "left")
```
